quotes.text: So infinite capacity isn't a defect and it isn't an attempt to mislead anyone. It's a boundary around what the planning logic is trying to do.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Reframes ERP's infinite capacity logic as a deliberate design boundary rather than a flaw.

quotes.text: So I'd be careful when people call Excel the problem. It survives because it lets a planner shape a local model around the factory they know
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Explains why spreadsheets persist in production planning instead of dismissing them.

quotes.text: So optimal doesn't mean perfect. It means the best feasible schedule against goals the business has actually stated with the reasons visible when one goal gives way to another.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Gives a practical definition of an optimal production schedule.

quotes.text: A prediction says this job may take longer, but a scheduling engine asks, given that risk, which legal sequence best meets the goals we've set?
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Clearly separates AI prediction from deterministic scheduling.

quotes.text: A schedule earns trust when it changes for visible reasons and stays still when it should.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: A memorable rule for schedule stability on the shop floor.

chapters.title: AI, stability and shop floor rules

takeaways: ERP plans material and dates against infinite capacity, so its dates are signals, not executable machine slots.
A feasible schedule must reserve real time on machines, tools and people, protect the bottleneck and account for sequence-dependent setups.
APS should own detailed scheduling with explicit rules and explanations, while Azure, Fabric and Power BI connect and analyze the data and AI supports rather than decides.
hook: Your ERP shows every order with a date, yet the shop floor knows by Monday morning that the plan will not survive the week. This episode explains why ERP cannot build an optimal production schedule, what finite scheduling and APS add, and where Microsoft data platforms and AI fit. For manufacturing planners, IT and operations leaders who want schedules people actually trust.
